shifts.headline: Lead-acid leader adding grid-storage systems and its own lithium cells
shifts.now: Amara Raja makes Amaron lead-acid batteries for cars, bikes, home inverters, telecom towers, data centres and industry, sold to vehicle makers, through more than 100,000 shops and to buyers in over 70 countries. Lead-acid batteries were ₹13,005cr, or 94%, of FY26 consolidated revenue of ₹13,814cr. The new-energy arm, which assembles lithium-ion battery packs and chargers for telecom towers and two- and three-wheelers, was ₹809cr (6%) and lost ₹135cr. In Q1 FY27 new energy was ₹209cr of ₹4,215cr, still about 5%.
shifts.future: By FY29 lead-acid will still be about four-fifths of sales, but new energy could be about a fifth, mostly from battery-storage systems (shipping-container-sized battery banks) for solar plants, the grid and businesses. The company is building a 10 GWh storage-system plant at Divitipally, for an initial ₹250–300cr, due to start in Q3–Q4 FY27; on the Q1 FY27 call (11 Aug 2026) the CFO said ‘within about 6-7 months we should be able to ramp it up’ to about 5 GWh, but added this was ‘based on the market demand’, not orders in hand. At his price of $100–120 per kWh, 5 GWh would be roughly ₹4,800–5,700cr of sales a year at about ₹95 to the dollar, at a thin 5–8% operating margin. Its first 2 GWh lithium-cell line (Giga-1) should start selling in H1 FY28, and FY27 capex is ₹1,700cr, of which ₹1,300cr goes to new energy. I assume the storage plant sells about half of that 5 GWh in FY29 and packs keep growing about 30% a year, which gives new energy about ₹4,000cr, or 19% of revenue against 6% in FY26: a real change, but just short of a ‘meaningful’ 15-point shift, and it rests on a plant with no disclosed orders.

shifts.headline: Phenol maker's polycarbonate bet starts only at the end of FY29
shifts.now: Deepak Nitrite makes basic and intermediate chemicals, mostly for Indian factories. Its Phenolics arm (₹5,401cr, 68% of FY26 segment revenue) turns benzene and propylene into phenol, acetone and IPA solvent, over half of India's supply, sold almost entirely at home to makers of resins, laminates, drugs, paints and agrochemicals. Advanced Intermediates (₹2,553cr, 32%) makes nitration chemicals such as sodium nitrite and building blocks for dyes, optical brighteners, agrochemicals and drugs, and exports about half of its output. Three years ago intermediates were 38% of revenue; Chinese price competition has since shrunk them in rupees.
shifts.future: The big change is a ₹11,500cr chain at Dahej that will make 165,000 tonnes a year of polycarbonate, the tough clear plastic used in car lights, electronics and sheets, from its own propylene, phenol and bisphenol-A, using a plant moved from Trinseo's German site. But management now targets polycarbonate start-up in 'H2' of FY28-29 with bisphenol-A 'a couple of months after' (Q1 FY27 call, 6 Aug 2026), later than the 'June 2028' it gave in May (Q4 FY26 call, 18 May 2026), and the new phenol plant waits for Petronet's propylene supply. About ₹1,200cr had been spent by August, ₹1,500–1,600cr more is planned in FY27, ₹6,800cr of debt is tied up and debt peaks at ₹8,000–8,500cr. Nearer term, the ₹735cr MIBK/MIBC solvents plant started on 6 August 2026, a ₹300cr chlorination and specialty plant on 29 September, and six or seven new intermediates reach regular supply from January 2027. So on my projection polycarbonate is only about 3% of FY29 revenue and the company still looks like a phenol and intermediates maker; at full use, probably from about FY31, the plant could earn roughly ₹3,000cr a year on my arithmetic, a quarter of the company, so the real shift comes after FY29.

Volume rises about 10% as the plant is pushed to a 4 lakh-tonne run-rate for about ₹70cr (Q1 FY27 call, 6 Aug 2026), and the MIBK/MIBC solvents plant (₹735cr, started 6 Aug 2026) adds downstream sales; the company has not said which segment will report MIBK/MIBC, so I place it here because it is made from the group's own acetone. I assume prices fall back to about FY26 levels after the Q1 FY27 war windfall (Q1 revenue ₹1,775cr, record 24% EBIT margin).

Q1 FY27 revenue of ₹804cr (+33%) is already a ₹3,200cr annual run-rate. New capacity: nitration and hydrogenation plants (from Q3 FY26), own nitric acid, a ₹300cr chlorination and specialty plant (29 Sep 2026), the multipurpose agrochemical-intermediates plant (Q2 FY27) and fluorination; six or seven new products in regular supply from January 2027 (Q1 FY27 call). I keep it to about 20% above the FY23 peak of ₹3,034cr because Chinese competition cut the segment by a sixth over FY23–FY26 and management says the 'red ocean' of price-cutting in its chemistries is only now easing.

Start-up targeted in H2 FY29 (Q1 FY27 call). I assume first resin around January 2029 and about 40% use for one quarter (roughly 16,000 tonnes at about ₹1.8 lakh a tonne) plus small compound sales (the compounds subsidiary had ₹29.5cr of income in FY26). If start-up slips six months, as most projects in this sector do, FY29 revenue is nil. Full use (165,000 tonnes) would be roughly ₹3,000cr a year, which I expect only from about FY31.

shifts.headline: Lead-acid giant starts making lithium cells; still a tenth by FY29
shifts.now: Exide is India's largest lead-acid battery maker, selling batteries for cars, bikes and trucks to more than 75 vehicle makers and to replacement buyers, plus home-inverter, solar, railway, telecom and industrial batteries, and it recycles its own lead. It reports a single segment; management says vehicles are about half of revenue (‘53:47’), home inverter batteries about ₹2,300cr and solar over ₹1,000cr. Of FY26 consolidated revenue of ₹17,995cr, the lithium subsidiary Exide Energy Solutions, which so far assembles packs from imported cells, was ₹158cr (about 1%) and lost ₹248cr; the other ₹17,838cr (99%) is lead-acid batteries and lead recycling.
shifts.future: Exide's 6 GWh lithium-cell plant in Bengaluru was commissioned on 23 September 2026 after about ₹5,600cr of spending: half cylindrical cells for electric two-wheelers, half LFP (lithium iron phosphate) cells for three-wheelers, telecom and storage. On the Q1 FY27 call (3 Aug 2026) the CEO said cell revenue starts in FY27, use will be 25–30% in the first year and ‘Demand will not be an issue’ because imported cells are simply being replaced; two-wheeler cells are in approval at three makers covering about 80% of that market, and a fourth line for storage and car cells is due around the end of FY27. Land and utilities are ready for a second 6 GWh, to be added ‘when the demand picks up’, and the board has approved ₹1,400cr more for the subsidiary in FY27. Lead-acid should keep growing about 10% a year, helped by the replacement wave from the post-GST car boom. I assume the plant sells about 2.8 GWh in FY29, under half its capacity, worth about ₹2,500cr, so lithium rises from 1% to about 10% of revenue: a real new business, but Exide stays a lead-acid company.

assumptions.why: Management guided ‘high-single to double-digit’ growth for FY27 and about 11% a year over five years, ‘(+/-1%)’ (Q4 FY26 call, 6 May 2026), and Q1 FY27 standalone growth was 17.6%. I use a little under 11% because FY23–FY26 consolidated lead-acid revenue grew only about 6% a year, the CEO warned the second half of FY27 faces a high base (3 Aug 2026), and telecom and e-rickshaw batteries (about 3% of revenue) keep moving to lithium. Core capex of about ₹500cr a year is removing bottlenecks in its five car-battery plants for the replacement wave expected 2.5–3 years after the post-GST car boom.

Phase 1 is 6 GWh at 25–30% use in its first year (CEO, Q1 FY27 call), which I take to about 45–50%, or 2.8 GWh, in FY29, at about ₹900cr of sales per GWh. That rate is my estimate, since management will not give one (‘let's not talk on crores. Let's talk on gigawatt hours’): it fits cells at roughly $70–90 per kWh with packs above that, and about one rupee of sales a year per rupee of the ₹5,600cr plant at full use. I stay well below the 85% use target because yields are still unproven, ICRA notes no take-or-pay contracts, two-wheeler approvals take months, and the plant already slipped from H2 FY26 to September 2026. No sales from a second phase before FY29.

shifts.managementAim: No revenue target. The CEO's yardstick is capacity: ‘6 gigawatt is our capacity of Phase 1’, with provision for 12 GWh ‘when the demand picks up’, and ‘put a number around that gigawatt hour and that should be our revenue’ (Q1 FY27 call, 3 Aug 2026). Targets: 25–30% use in the first year, then 85% use at 90% yield before it will discuss margins (Q4 FY26 call, 6 May 2026); 50–60% of cell materials sourced in India within 2–3 years; and lead-acid growth of about 11% a year over five years.

shifts.headline: Car and window films now three-quarters; further shift is modest
shifts.now: Garware Hi-Tech Films makes specialty polyester films, from raw chips to finished film, at Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, and sells about three-quarters abroad, 44% to the US alone. Sun-control window film for cars and buildings is its main line, about ₹1,060cr or 50% of FY26 revenue of ₹2,120cr; clear paint-protection film for car bodies brought about ₹509cr (24%), and industrial films such as shrink labels, electrical insulation and packaging film about ₹551cr (26%). Three years ago industrial films were half the business and paint-protection film only about 5%.
shifts.future: By FY29 Garware should look much like today, only bigger: the big change in its mix happened between FY23 and FY26. Management guides “over ₹2,500cr” of revenue in FY27, 15–20% growth a year after that and about ₹3,500cr “in three to four years” (Q1 FY27 call, 7 Aug 2026). Most of that growth comes from sun-control film: the existing lines were 75–80% full in May 2026, and a ₹191–192cr line adding about 30% more capacity (1,200 lakh sq ft a year, ₹500–550cr of sales at peak) is due in H1 FY28 by the company's date and June 2028 by CARE's. The ₹118cr TPU film line due in Q3 FY27 mainly feeds Garware's own paint-protection film (about 75% of its output), so it should lift margins by an expected 1.5–2 points in FY28 rather than create a large new line. On my numbers sun-control film rises to about 55% of revenue, paint-protection film holds at about a quarter and industrial films slip to about 20%.

assumptions.why: FY26 sun-control volume was 3,031 lakh sq ft (CARE) against 4,200 of capacity, and management said in May 2026 that the lines would be full by FY28, which is roughly 25–30% more volume. The new 1,200 lakh sq ft line (peak sales ₹500–550cr) might add about ₹200cr in FY29, as its start date is uncertain (H1 FY28 per the company, June 2028 per CARE) and some of it will be used for paint-protection film. Architectural and home film, about a quarter of sun-control sales and growing 25–30% a year by management's account, lift the mix. Guidance looks reachable for FY27, but I assume sun-control growth slows in FY28 while capacity is tight.

Capacity doubled to 60 million sq ft when the second line started in Q2 FY26; the old line runs near 100% and the new one about 60% (Q1 FY27 call), so filling it adds roughly a quarter. The TPU line (360 lakh sq ft a year) sends only about a quarter of its output to outside sales of new products, so management's hope that TPU becomes “beyond ₹500cr” in three years needs more capex and is not in my numbers. Growth is held back by its largest US customer's talk of making film in-house and by cheap Chinese and Korean imports (an anti-dumping duty has only been recommended). It grew only about 6% a year from the roughly ₹450cr an analyst cited for FY24 on the Q4 FY24 call to FY26.

No new industrial capacity is planned (42,000 tonnes a year); volumes of some industrial products fell in FY26 (CARE), and the company's capex and marketing go to consumer films. Prices mostly follow raw materials, so I assume low single-digit growth.

shifts.headline: Truck and tractor crankshaft maker moving into heavy industrial parts
shifts.now: Happy Forgings, based in Ludhiana, forges and machines heavy crankshafts, axle beams and transmission parts; 89% of FY26 sales were fully machined parts. Of FY26 revenue of ₹1,546cr, trucks made up 37%, tractors 32%, industrial engines and machines (power generation, wind, rail, oil and gas, data centres) 14%, off-highway machines 11% and cars 6%. It sells to Indian and European truck and tractor makers and to global engine makers; about a quarter of revenue is exported directly or indirectly.
shifts.future: By FY29 I expect industrial parts to be about 22% and cars about 10% of a roughly ₹2,375cr business, with trucks and tractors falling from 69% to 58% of revenue: a real but modest shift. The new work comes from an order book worth about ₹950cr of extra yearly revenue once ramped up over two to three years, roughly 40% industrial and 25–30% cars, with 60% for export (Q1 FY27 call, 5 Aug 2026). The key capex is a heavy line for parts of 250 kg to 3 tonnes, inside a ₹650cr programme, which finishes installation by March 2027, starts selling in FY28 after 6–9 months of customer testing, and should 'start contributing meaningfully from FY29'; about ₹250cr of the order book is heavy parts for data-centre generator engines. Management aims for industrials at 30–31% of revenue and trucks at 27% (Q4 FY26 call, 22 May 2026), but I stop short because the heavy line ramps only late in FY28 and its truck forecast for FY27 has already slipped.

shifts.headline: Battery maker turned Kavach supplier; fuzes and e-drives come next
shifts.now: HBL makes Kavach, the Indian Railways system that brakes trains automatically to stop collisions, plus train-management systems, and specialised batteries: nickel-cadmium, lead-acid and lithium batteries for railways, telecom, data centres, oil and gas and export, and batteries for aircraft, missiles and submarines. In FY26 the electronics segment, mostly Kavach, was ₹1,626cr (49%) of ₹3,311cr of consolidated segment revenue, industrial batteries ₹1,416cr (43%), defence and aviation batteries ₹212cr (6%) and other lines ₹57cr (2%). Three years earlier industrial batteries alone were three-quarters of sales; Kavach orders from a single buyer, the railways, changed that in FY26.
shifts.future: The big shift has already happened; the next three years are about whether new lines take over as Kavach fades. HBL holds no earnings calls, but the chairman's FY26 annual report (Sep 2026) says Kavach, almost half of FY26 sales, should be about the same share in FY27, that ‘sales will continue to be good in FY 27 and FY 28’, and that ‘both sales and PBT could decline from FY 29 onwards’ as competition grows; in January 2026 HBL lost a 6,300-unit locomotive tender on price, though it won a ₹1,714cr locomotive order in May. The growth he points to is electronic fuzes for ammunition (grenade fuzes already sell to the Home Ministry; Army and 155 mm artillery approvals are expected in 2027), electric drive trains for 55-tonne trucks (approval by March 2027, pilot sales from July 2027, already nine months late) and for boats through a joint venture with Cochin Shipyard, and nickel-cadmium and data-centre batteries whose capacity is being expanded. Capex is small, ₹150cr in FY26 from its own cash. Management's ‘not a prediction’ scenario is more than ₹5,000cr of sales in FY30; I expect about ₹3,900cr in FY29, with electronics down to about 39%, defence (batteries plus fuzes) up from 6% to about 14%, and batteries back as the largest line at about 45%. That flip in the largest line comes from Kavach shrinking, not a new business, so I call the shift modest.

shifts.headline: Wagon maker building a big wheel plant, plus batteries
shifts.now: Jupiter Wagons builds railway freight wagons, about 80% of its current wagon orders for private owners such as JSW and the rest for Indian Railways, plus load bodies for trucks, containers and rail crossings. Through subsidiaries it also makes wheelsets and axles at Aurangabad, freight brakes (Stone India, from July 2026), battery-storage systems and small electric trucks. In FY26 (consolidated revenue ₹2,916cr, a weak year when wheelset shortages cut wagon output by over a third) wagons were about 69% of revenue, wheels and axles sold outside the group 12%, truck bodies and containers 14%, batteries and EVs 1% and other parts 3%. Three years earlier (FY23) it was almost a pure wagon and truck-body maker, with wagons 79%.
shifts.future: Management targets about ₹9,000cr of revenue by FY28–FY29 (CFO, investor conference call, 30 Sep 2026) and, earlier, ₹10,000cr by 2030 at a 15%+ margin with wagons only half of sales (MD, Q4 FY26 call, 1 Jun 2026), against about ₹3,000cr expected again in FY27. The main engine is a ₹2,500–2,600cr forged wheel and axle plant in Odisha (100,000 wheelsets a year, half meant for export; Italy's Lucchini and SIMEST pay about ₹290cr for 25%), which management says will bring ₹2,500–3,000cr of revenue once both lines run (Q1 FY27 call, 18 Aug 2026); the axle line is due by March 2027 and the wheel line by March 2028, and 'we will not see much volume in FY28 apart from some axle sales' (30 Sep 2026), so FY29 is its first full year. Battery storage has a ₹500cr order book, but ₹400cr of it is a 15-year build-own-operate project, where Jupiter owns the batteries and is paid over the years rather than booking a one-off sale. Wagons wait on a Railways tender with no date; Jupiter expects about 7,000 wagons a year once it comes. I expect about ₹4,500cr in FY29, with wagons down to about 56% of sales and wheels up to about 20%: a meaningful shift, but about half of management's target.

shifts.now: Kaynes is a contract electronics maker: it builds circuit boards, cables and complete electronic products to other companies' designs, mainly for industrial and EV makers (55% of FY26 revenue) and car makers (25%), plus IT, rail, medical and aerospace customers, from plants across India and in Canada and the US. Of FY26 revenue of ₹3,626cr, contract manufacturing was ₹2,655cr (73%, including about ₹300cr from the overseas units) and smart electricity meters, from Iskraemeco (now Gridcrest) bought in 2024, ₹971cr (27%); the meter business also installs and services meters for state utilities, which pay slowly. Three years ago Kaynes was a ₹1,126cr pure contract manufacturer.
shifts.future: Kaynes is building two new businesses: a ₹3,307cr chip assembly and test plant (OSAT) at Sanand, where 50% central and 20% state grants cover the qualifying cost, and a ₹1,400cr plant for advanced bare circuit boards (PCBs) in Chennai (FY26 annual report). About ₹1,200cr had been spent by August 2026, ₹300cr more each is planned for FY27, and both should start billing in Q3 FY27, a quarter late, with ₹450–500cr of combined FY27 revenue (Q1 FY27 call, 8 Aug 2026), down from the ₹550–700cr implied in May (Q4 FY26 call, 14 May 2026). Management says the chip plant has over ₹2,500cr of revenue visibility over five years, one large global buyer has asked for the board plant's 'entire capacity', and its stated aim is for chip packaging alone to be 30% of group revenue within four to five years. Meanwhile it is shrinking smart meters on purpose until state utilities pay the ₹1,311cr they owe, and may sell the installation side. On my projection the two plants reach about a fifth of FY29 revenue, not the third management talks about, because they are late, the customer list is thin and Kaynes missed its FY26 revenue guidance by about 20%.

shifts.headline: Engine maker adding data-centre gensets and exports; the mix barely moves
shifts.now: Kirloskar Oil makes diesel and gas engines and generator sets (from 1 kW to 10 MW) for shops, homes, offices, factories and data centres, and engines for tractors, construction machines, trains, ships and the navy; it also sells spares and service, makes pumps through KOEL Fluid Dynamics and owns a lender, Arka Fincap. Of FY26 consolidated revenue of ₹7,701cr, engines and gensets sold in India were about 53% (₹4,105cr), spares and service 13% (₹968cr), engine exports 8% (₹613cr), pumps 15% (₹1,138cr) and Arka's lending 11% (₹877cr). It sold over 50,000 gensets in FY26, up 41% against a market up 18%, and its share of large sets above 750 kVA is now 'approaching double digits'.
shifts.future: Management aims for $2bn (about ₹16,000cr) of consolidated revenue by FY30 (FY26 annual report) and says growth is led by large engines, though from a small base, with growth 'right across' the range (Q1 FY27 call, 7 Aug 2026). It is spending ₹700cr to add 50,000 engines a year at Kagal from April 2027 (today's capacity is about 1.35 lakh engines), and ₹1,400cr over the next two years on a new building for 20,000 mostly large engines that it says could bring 'close to 5,000 crores, 6,000 crores' of revenue at full use (Q4 FY26 call, 14 May 2026), though only from about FY29. Big orders back this: 96 large OptiPrime gensets (192 MW) for data-centre builder HyperNext, billed this year with five to six years of maintenance, and ₹798cr of gensets for the Nuclear Power Corporation, billed from FY27 to 2029; a new defence subsidiary and a 6 MW navy engine add to the large-engine line. Abroad, it has teamed up with Germany's DEUTZ to sell a small engine in Europe and North America and set up a Dutch subsidiary, but exports fell 11% in Q1 FY27 as the Middle East war hit shipments. Because the company does not report large engines separately and its India engine sales are growing as fast, on my projection the mix barely moves by FY29; the one change that would reshape it, separating Arka, has no date ('it takes time', Q1 FY27 call).

shifts.headline: Truck-parts forger edging into railways and industry, slowly
shifts.now: Ramkrishna Forgings hammers hot steel into heavy parts such as front axle beams, crankshafts and ring-rolled parts, and now also makes castings, mostly for truck makers in India, the US and Europe. In FY26 (standalone revenue ₹3,755cr; consolidated ₹4,238cr) Indian vehicle makers took 47% of sales, exported vehicle parts 27%, railways 7.5% and mining, farm, industrial and energy customers 19%. Three years earlier exported vehicle parts were 36% and railways under 3%, so the past shift has been from US trucks towards Indian vehicles more than away from trucks. Its rail-wheel plant with Titagarh is a separate joint venture, so wheel sales will not show in its revenue, only its share of the profit.
shifts.future: Management now targets ₹8,000cr of revenue by FY29, a year later than first promised, which means 22–25% growth a year ('we are on track for an 8,000-crore target for FY29', Q1 FY27 call, 24 Jul 2026). The growth is meant to come from filling plants already built (over ₹800cr spent in FY25–FY26; presses at 60% and castings at 79% use in Q1 FY27), with FY27 capex held to about ₹350cr and no big new spending before end-FY28. Railways (assembled bogie frames, metro parts) are to reach a double-digit share, exports to grow 20%+ in FY27, and non-auto to pass 30% of revenue by FY30 (FY26 annual report), while aerospace forgings in titanium and Inconel have 'zero exposure' today and are 'at least 2 years' from meaningful revenue (Q1 FY27 call). At the 75–80% use management expects before new capex, the existing plants support only about ₹5,400–5,700cr of consolidated sales at today's prices, so I expect about ₹5,200cr standalone (roughly ₹5,700cr consolidated) in FY29. Truck and other vehicle parts would still be about 70% of sales, so the shift is modest.

shifts.headline: Former textile group, now auto parts with a growing aerospace arm
shifts.now: After demerging its textile and property businesses in 2024–25, Raymond Ltd is a holding company that owns about two-thirds of two engineering businesses. JK Maini Precision Technology (₹1,667cr, 81% of FY26 engineering revenue) makes ring gears, flexplates and drivetrain parts for car and truck makers, including hybrids, plus JK Files steel files and hand tools; over 60% is exported. JK Maini Global Aerospace (₹392cr, 19%) makes aero-engine parts for the world's big engine makers, including 350+ parts for the LEAP engine, plus landing-gear and structural parts. A further ₹153cr of job work and a small charter airline ('Others') is left out of the figures below.
shifts.future: Three years ago the listed Raymond was mainly a textile, apparel and property company; it bought control of Maini Precision only in FY24, and on a pro-forma basis aerospace was about 11% of today's engineering businesses. By FY29 I expect aerospace to be about a quarter of a roughly ₹2,970cr engineering business. Management says 'we have committed 25% growth' in aerospace (Q1 FY27 call, 7 Aug 2026) and delivered 40% in Q1, and parts already under contract schedule about ₹555cr of aerospace revenue for 2029 within a ₹5,960cr ten-year order book. But the existing Bommasandra plant tops out at about ₹650cr, so growth beyond that needs the ₹510cr Gudipalli plant in Andhra Pradesh, due to start commercial production in late 2027 and to contribute mainly from FY29 after up to six months of customer approvals. The precision and auto arm, four times larger, is guided at 12–14% a year and gets its own ₹430cr plant at the same site, so the mix moves only about six points unless an acquisition, funded partly by ₹331cr of promoter warrants, changes it.

shifts.headline: Auto-parts forger adding aerospace and chip-equipment parts
shifts.now: Sansera forges and machines precision metal parts. In FY26, 70% of its ₹3,498cr revenue came from engine parts such as connecting rods, crankshafts and rocker arms for motorcycles, scooters, cars and trucks, sold to Maruti, Bajaj, TVS and global vehicle makers. Another 13% came from parts that fit any vehicle or go into electric and hybrid ones. The rest, about a sixth, was non-auto work: aerospace, defence and chip-equipment parts (ADS, ₹336cr or 10%) and parts for off-road, farm and industrial machines (₹238cr or 7%).
shifts.future: By FY29 I expect aerospace, defence and chip-equipment parts (ADS) to be about a fifth of a roughly ₹5,700cr business, double today's share, while auto parts still make up about three-quarters. Management guides ADS revenue of ₹550–600cr in FY27, up 75–80%, and holds an ADS backlog of about ₹5,750cr that it says 'is mandatorily executable … by FY 2031' (Q1 FY27 call, 13 Aug 2026), including a chip-equipment order worth about ₹1,250cr over five years whose revenue starts in 2027 and peaks in 2029. To deliver it, Sansera is commissioning an 80,000 sq ft hangar and an in-house surface-treatment plant in Bengaluru from Q3 FY27, moving defence into its own building and negotiating a 100,000 sq ft build-to-suit plant due about ten months later, with a plan for capacity worth about ₹3,500cr of ADS revenue by FY31; each ₹1 of ADS plant earns about ₹2–2.25 of sales. Auto is not standing still: engine parts grew 21% in Q1 FY27 and about three-quarters of Q1 capex went to auto lines such as new crankshaft and connecting-rod capacity at Pantnagar and Manesar, so the mix moves only about ten points.

shifts.headline: From furniture parts to pen injectors for weight-loss drugs
shifts.now: Shaily moulds precision plastic parts to order at Vadodara, with a design arm in the UK. Its biggest line is still consumer goods – mostly furniture and home-furnishing parts, plus toys and FMCG parts, sold to large global retailers and brands – at ₹511cr, 52% of FY26 revenue of ₹991cr. Healthcare, mainly pen injectors that drug makers fill with insulin and the weight-loss drug semaglutide, brought ₹393cr (40%), and industrial parts for appliances, cars and power tools ₹87cr (9%). In the June 2026 quarter healthcare overtook consumer for the first time, at 51% of revenue.
shifts.future: By FY29 Shaily should be mainly a drug-device maker. Management expects to make “beyond 36 million” pens in FY27 (Q1 FY27 call, 10 Aug 2026) against 23.5 million in FY26, and about 50 million in FY28 (Q4 FY26 call, 20 May 2026). The capacity is being built: two new 25-million-pen lines (one running since March 2026, the other due by end-September 2026) take India pen capacity to about 75 million a year, and a ₹300–350cr plant in Abu Dhabi for about 75 million more pens and auto-injectors should be producing by the end of FY28, with 50–55% of it already committed (Q3 FY26 call, 13 Feb 2026; Q1 FY27 call). The consumer business is not expected to grow this year, while electronics parts and semiconductor chip trays start small from late FY27. On my numbers healthcare reaches about ₹950cr, close to 60% of revenue, while consumer stays near ₹500cr.

shifts.headline: Still mainly a drum maker; gas cylinders grow from a small base
shifts.now: Time Technoplast makes plastic industrial packaging – drums, jerry cans and pails for chemical, paint and FMCG companies – in India and ten other countries, plus 1,000-litre caged bulk tanks (IBCs), lightweight composite gas cylinders, plastic pipes and a few other products. Of FY26 revenue of ₹6,114cr, drums, cans and pails were ₹3,744cr (61%), IBCs ₹808cr (13%), composite LPG, CNG and oxygen cylinders ₹762cr (12%), pipes, batteries, matting and auto parts ₹629cr (10%) and MOX tarpaulin film ₹171cr (3%). The company calls IBCs, cylinders and MOX film its value-added products: 29% of revenue in FY26, up from 23% in FY23.
shifts.future: By FY29 Time should look much as it does now. Management guides 15% volume growth a year: 11–13% for packaging, 25–30% for composite products, 20–25% for PE pipes and 10–12% for MOX film and other products (Q1 FY27 call, 6 Aug 2026), and wants composites to grow “by over 25%” a year for three years (Q4 FY26 call, 29 May 2026). Capex is about ₹350cr in FY27 (₹47cr of Q1's ₹75cr went to IBCs and composites), then ₹200–250cr a year; the new Mora plant has more than doubled CNG cascade capacity to 1,080 a year, and Silvassa's IBC capacity doubles to 300,000 a year by March 2027. Even so, packaging is so large that on my numbers composite cylinders rise only from about 12% to about 16% of revenue, and value-added products from 29% to about a third.

Working capital is stretched (about 110 days, with imported carbon fibre stocked for six months) and composite contracts are fixed-price for a year.
Pipes depend on government contractors, who refused price rises in Q1 FY27.
shifts.confidenceWhy: Capacity for the value-added lines is built or funded, but the composite order book covers only about three months, so the FY29 mix is mostly an extrapolation of steady trends; because packaging is so large, even a big beat or miss in composites moves the mix by only a few points.

shifts.headline: Wagon builder turning into a metro and Vande Bharat train maker
shifts.now: Titagarh builds freight wagons and their steel castings for Indian Railways and private owners, and passenger trains: metro cars for Bengaluru, Gujarat, Mumbai and Pune, Vande Bharat sleeper trains (with BHEL), and the propulsion systems and traction motors that drive them. In FY26 (consolidated revenue ₹3,186cr) freight wagons and other heavy engineering, including a small shipyard, were 83% of revenue and passenger trains 17% (₹539cr). Three years earlier passenger work was already 19% thanks to Pune Metro deliveries, then fell to 7% in FY25 before recovering, so the big change is still ahead. Its 49% share of a rail-wheel plant with Ramkrishna Forgings is a joint venture: only its share of the profit will show, not the wheel sales.
shifts.future: Passenger work is already 81% of the ₹12,865cr rail order book (491 metro cars and 1,280 Vande Bharat cars) and was 31% of revenue in Q1 FY27; management says passenger 'will overtake the freight business and become the dominant part of the business' (Q1 FY27 call, 14 Aug 2026). It plans capacity for 850+ coaches a year by 2028–29, which it says is worth ₹8,500–9,000cr a year if full, using 40 extra acres at Uttarpara with a 1.6km test track, an in-house aluminium coach line due by Q1 FY28 and FY26 capex of ₹368cr. Freight has been cut to 600–650 wagons a month while the Railways' tender for about one lakh wagons is awaited, so I expect it to grow only modestly once orders return. I expect passenger revenue of about ₹2,900cr in FY29, close to half of a ~₹6,100cr business, but below the company's own plan because the coach ramp keeps slipping (63 coaches in FY26 against 100–120 planned). The ~₹600cr Falta shipyard adds a little from FY28.

assumptions.why: Built car by car: about 230 metro cars at roughly ₹9cr each and 170 Vande Bharat sleeper cars at roughly ₹4cr each (Titagarh keeps about 51% of each car's value; BHEL the rest), plus about ₹150cr of propulsion and traction motors. Roughly ₹4,400cr of metro work (491 cars) and all 1,280 Vande Bharat cars are already on order. I use only about 60–65% of the strategic plan's car numbers (275–300 metro cars in FY28 rising towards 500–550; 192 Vande Bharat cars in FY28 and 288 in FY29; plan of 13 Nov 2025) because FY26 delivered 63 cars against 100–120 planned and FY27 is tracking about 180 (30 in Q1 plus 45–50 a quarter) against 200. FY29 also needs about ₹1,000–1,500cr of new metro orders from the ₹16,365cr pipeline the company lists, as the current metro book runs out during FY29.

About 7,800 wagons at ~₹37 lakh each (FY26: 7,019 wagons for ₹2,604cr; FY25: 9,431 for ₹3,492cr) plus ~₹250cr from the shipyard (₹470cr order book over 30 months; new Falta yard running from Q1–Q2 FY28). Output averages about 650 a month in FY29, a blend of the Railways' big tender arriving during FY28 (800–1,000 a month) and further delay (500–600 a month on private orders); management calls 600 a month a bad year and 1,000 a good one (Q4 FY26 call, 1 Jun 2026). drivers.text: Wagon output deliberately cut to 600–650 a month (capacity 1,000) until the Railways issues its large wagon tender, which management says can be 'deferred by a few months or a couple of quarters, but it cannot be stopped'.

risks: The coach ramp keeps slipping: 63 cars in FY26 against 100–120 planned, and FY27 is tracking about 180 against 200; another slip pushes the passenger share out by a year.

The Vande Bharat sleeper prototype is due only at the end of Q3 or start of Q4 FY27 after an earlier design change (16 to 24 cars); trial delays would hold back the largest order, on which Titagarh keeps only about half the value.
The Railways can take work in-house: the tender for 2,856 Mumbai suburban 'Vande Metro' cars was cancelled and given to its own factory.
After FY28 the metro line needs new orders against Alstom, BEML and others; without them FY29 passenger revenue falls short.
Freight depends on a tender with no date; the wagon book of ~5,300 wagons runs out in FY27, which could leave the plant at 600 wagons a month or less.

Cash and balance sheet strain: the cash cycle stretched to 113 days, Titagarh has a ₹504cr undertaking for the wheel venture's loans, and its auditor flagged control weaknesses after the Firema write-offs.
shifts.confidenceWhy: Most of the FY29 passenger figure is already on order and capacity is being built, but the company has delivered well short of its own coach plans and the freight figure rests on a Railways tender with no date.
